words.plain: Compared by what money can actually buy, incomes are similar.
words.model: At purchasing power parity, incomes are similar.

words.meaning: The idea that beyond a point, higher tax rates raise less revenue.
words.everyday: Like a shop pricing so high that fewer buy and takings fall.
words.work: The Laffer curve was used to justify top-rate cuts.
words.gap: Supporters cite the ___ when cutting taxes.
words.plain: Very high tax rates can actually bring in less money.

words.meaning: When frozen tax thresholds pull more income into higher bands as wages rise.
words.everyday: Like a height limit on a ride that stays fixed while children grow.
words.work: Freezing allowances raises billions through fiscal drag.
words.gap: Frozen thresholds cause ___.
words.plain: More people pay higher tax because the bands haven't risen with pay.

words.meaning: A market where one supplier is most efficient because of huge fixed costs.
words.everyday: Like water pipes: one network is cheaper than two side by side.
words.work: Railways are a natural monopoly, so they're regulated.
words.gap: The national grid is a ___.
words.plain: It makes sense for one firm to run it because duplicating it is too costly.

words.meaning: Prices that don't adjust quickly to changes in supply or demand.
words.everyday: Like a café that won't reprint its menu every time milk prices move.
words.work: Sticky prices explain why recessions hit output, not just prices.
words.gap: Because of ___, wages don't fall quickly in a slump.
words.plain: Prices don't change quickly even when demand drops.

words.meaning: When a country spends more abroad, on imports and income payments, than it earns.
words.everyday: Like a household spending more on outside services than it earns from them.
words.work: The UK has run a current account deficit for decades.
words.gap: A large ___ makes the pound vulnerable.
words.plain: The country buys more from abroad than it sells.
words.model: The country runs a current account deficit.

words.meaning: The ratio of export prices to import prices.
words.everyday: Like how many hours you must work to afford a weekly shop.
words.work: Higher oil prices worsened Europe's terms of trade.
words.gap: Falling copper prices hurt Chile's ___.
words.plain: Our exports buy fewer imports than before.
words.model: Our terms of trade have worsened.

words.meaning: Money rapidly leaving a country because of risk or policy.
words.everyday: Like customers emptying their accounts after a rumour about the bank.
words.work: The election triggered capital flight.
words.gap: Currency controls aim to stop ___.
words.plain: Investors pulled their money out of the country fast.

words.meaning: "Bad money drives out good": people spend debased money and hoard the better kind.
words.everyday: Like spending your scruffy notes first and keeping the crisp ones.
words.work: Gresham's law explains why silver coins vanished.
words.gap: When coins were debased, ___ kicked in.
words.plain: People spent the worse coins and kept the better ones.

words.meaning: Rising costs in labour-heavy services that can't easily boost productivity.
words.everyday: A string quartet needs four players today, just as in 1800, but must pay modern wages.
words.work: Baumol's cost disease explains rising care costs.
words.gap: Education costs rise faster than inflation due to ___.
words.plain: Services that can't be automated keep getting more expensive.

words.meaning: When government borrowing pushes up rates and reduces private investment.
words.everyday: Like the council booking every slot at the sports hall so clubs can't.
words.work: Critics warned the deficit would cause crowding out.
words.gap: Heavy borrowing risks ___ of business investment.
words.plain: Government borrowing leaves less money for private firms.

words.meaning: When interest rates are near zero and cutting them no longer stimulates spending.
words.everyday: Like pushing on a string: lowering the price of borrowing doesn't make anyone borrow.
words.work: Japan was stuck in a liquidity trap for years.
words.gap: With rates at zero, the economy fell into a ___.
words.plain: Rates are so low that cutting them further does nothing.

words.meaning: The observed trade-off between unemployment and inflation.
words.everyday: Like a tight job market forcing employers to raise pay, then prices.
words.work: The Phillips curve looked flat in the 2010s.
words.gap: A flat ___ means jobs can grow without inflation.
words.plain: Low unemployment usually comes with higher inflation.

words.meaning: The unemployment rate below which inflation tends to rise.
words.everyday: Like a speed limit for the jobs market.
words.work: The Bank thinks unemployment is below the NAIRU.
words.gap: Unemployment below the ___ pushes wages up.
words.plain: If unemployment falls below a certain level, inflation picks up.

words.meaning: When a resource boom raises the currency and hurts other exporters.
words.everyday: Like a town's tourism boom pushing up rents until local workshops close.
words.work: North Sea oil gave Britain a touch of Dutch disease.
words.gap: The gas boom brought ___ to manufacturing.
words.plain: The oil boom made the currency strong and killed off factories.

words.meaning: A tax set to equal the harm an activity causes to others.
words.everyday: Like charging the noisy neighbour for everyone's earplugs.
words.work: A carbon tax is a Pigouvian tax.
words.gap: The sugar levy is a ___.
words.plain: The tax makes polluters pay for the damage they cause.

words.meaning: The unexplained slowdown in UK productivity growth since 2008.
words.everyday: Like a team with better tools that somehow doesn't get more done.
words.work: The productivity puzzle explains flat UK wages.
words.gap: Economists still debate the ___.
words.plain: We don't know why output per worker stopped growing.

words.meaning: When a temporary shock leaves lasting damage, such as long-term unemployment.
words.everyday: Like a sprain that leaves a permanent limp.
words.work: Hysteresis means recessions can lower growth for good.
words.gap: Long recessions cause ___ in the labour market.
words.plain: The recession left permanent damage even after it ended.

words.meaning: A luxury good that people want more of as its price rises.
words.everyday: Like a handbag that sells better because it costs £5,000.
words.work: Luxury brands price as Veblen goods.
words.gap: Designer watches behave like a ___.
words.plain: People want it more because it's expensive.

words.meaning: A staple that poor households buy more of when its price rises, as they can't afford alternatives.
words.everyday: Like eating more rice when it gets dearer because meat is now out of reach.
words.work: Rice in poor Chinese provinces behaved like a Giffen good.
words.gap: When bread prices rose, it acted as a ___.
words.plain: People bought more of it as it got pricier because they couldn't afford anything else.

words.meaning: The argument that historical relationships break down when policy changes people's expectations.
words.everyday: Like a shortcut that stops working once everyone hears about it.
words.work: By the Lucas critique, the old model can't predict the new policy.
words.gap: The ___ warns against using past data to judge new policy.
words.plain: Old patterns won't hold because people react to the new policy.

words.meaning: As income rises, the share spent on food falls.
words.everyday: Like a student spending most on food, but a CEO hardly noticing the grocery bill.
words.work: Engel's law explains the shift to services.
words.gap: By ___, richer households spend a smaller share on food.
words.plain: As people get richer, food takes up less of their budget.

words.meaning: A country can't have a fixed exchange rate, free capital flows and independent monetary policy all at once.
words.everyday: Like wanting a cheap, fast and perfect builder: pick two.
words.work: The impossible trinity forced Britain out of the ERM.
words.gap: Hong Kong's peg reflects the ___.
words.plain: You can't fix the currency, allow free capital flows and set your own rates.

words.meaning: One hundredth of a percentage point (0.01%).
words.everyday: Like measuring a race in hundredths of a second.
words.work: The Bank raised rates by 25 basis points.
words.gap: Rates rose by 50 ___s, or half a percentage point.
words.plain: The rate went up by a quarter of a percentage point.
words.model: The rate went up 25 basis points.

words.meaning: A graph of interest rates on bonds across different maturities.
words.everyday: Like a price list showing how much more you earn for locking savings away longer.
words.work: The yield curve steepened after the budget.
words.gap: Investors watch the ___ for recession signals.
words.plain: The chart of interest rates from short to long bonds has changed shape.
words.model: The yield curve has changed shape.

words.meaning: A rapid price rise that forces short sellers to buy back shares, pushing it higher.
words.everyday: Like everyone who bet against a team rushing to change sides as it starts winning.
words.work: GameStop's surge was a short squeeze.
words.gap: Retail buyers triggered a ___.
words.plain: People who bet on the share falling had to buy it, sending it higher.

words.meaning: A bond from a riskier borrower that pays higher interest; also called junk.
words.everyday: Like lending to a friend with a patchy record in return for a bigger thank-you.
words.work: The buyout was funded with high-yield bonds.
words.gap: The company issued a ___ at 9%.
words.plain: They borrowed by selling risky bonds that pay high interest.

words.meaning: A credit rating of BBB- or above, signalling a relatively safe borrower.
words.everyday: Like a reliable friend you'd lend money to without worrying.
words.work: A downgrade below investment grade forces some funds to sell.
words.gap: Pension funds can only hold ___ bonds.
words.plain: The bond is rated safe enough for cautious funds.

words.meaning: Buying a company mostly with borrowed money, secured on the target's own assets.
words.everyday: Like buying a house with a huge mortgage and making the rent pay it off.
words.work: The private equity firm did a leveraged buyout of the retailer.
words.gap: The chain was taken private in a ___.
words.plain: They bought the company with mostly borrowed money.

words.meaning: A firm that always quotes prices to buy and sell, providing liquidity.
words.everyday: Like a bureau de change that always buys and sells currency.
words.work: Market makers widened spreads during the sell-off.
words.gap: A ___ profits from the gap between buying and selling prices.
words.plain: A firm that's always ready to buy or sell keeps trading smooth.

words.meaning: The gap between the highest buying price and the lowest selling price.
words.everyday: Like the difference between what a pawnshop pays for a watch and what it sells it for.
words.work: Small caps have a wide bid-ask spread.
words.gap: A wide ___ means the share is hard to trade.
words.plain: The gap between buying and selling prices is big.

words.meaning: A drop in existing owners' percentage stake when new shares are issued.
words.everyday: Like adding more slices to a pizza: same pizza, smaller slices.
words.work: The funding round caused 20% dilution.
words.gap: Employees worry about ___ when new shares are issued.
words.plain: Our share of the company shrank when new investors came in.

words.meaning: Earnings before interest, tax, depreciation and amortisation: a rough measure of operating profit.
words.everyday: Like judging a café's takings before rent on the coffee machine and loan repayments.
words.work: Buyout debt is often set as a multiple of EBITDA.
words.gap: The firm trades at ten times ___.
words.plain: Profit before interest, tax and accounting write-downs was £5m.

words.meaning: A company's total value: equity plus debt minus cash.
words.everyday: Like the real price of a house including the mortgage you take over.
words.work: Compare enterprise value to EBITDA, not market cap.
words.gap: The deal valued the firm at a £2bn ___.
words.plain: Including its debt and cash, the company is worth £2bn.

words.meaning: A share's price divided by its earnings per share.
words.everyday: Like how many years of profit you'd pay to buy a shop.
words.work: Tech firms trade on a high price-to-earnings ratio.
words.gap: A ___ of 40 suggests high growth expectations.
words.plain: Investors pay 30 times this year's profit for the shares.
words.model: The shares trade on a price-to-earnings ratio of 30.

words.meaning: Returns above what the market or a benchmark would have delivered.
words.everyday: Like a runner beating the time the conditions would predict.
words.work: The fund charges high fees but shows no alpha.
words.gap: The manager claims to generate ___.
words.plain: The fund beat the market by 2% after accounting for risk.

words.meaning: A demand for more collateral when leveraged positions lose value.
words.everyday: Like a pawnshop asking for more items because your watch is now worth less.
words.work: The fund faced margin calls as prices fell.
words.gap: The trader got a ___ and had to sell.
words.plain: The broker demanded more money because the trades lost value.
words.model: The trader got a margin call.

words.meaning: A UK government bond.
words.everyday: Like an IOU from the Treasury.
words.work: Gilt yields jumped after the mini-budget.
words.gap: Pension funds hold lots of long-dated ___s.
words.plain: The government borrows by selling bonds to investors.

words.meaning: The fixed interest payment a bond pays each year.
words.everyday: Like the rent a lodger pays on a fixed schedule.
words.work: The bond pays a 4% coupon twice a year.
words.gap: The bond's ___ is 5% a year.
words.plain: The bond pays 3% interest each year.

words.meaning: A rare, unpredictable event with huge impact.
words.everyday: Like a meteor hitting your house: nobody planned for it.
words.work: The pandemic was treated as a black swan.
words.gap: Models failed to anticipate the ___.
words.plain: A rare, unexpected event caused huge losses.
words.model: A black swan caused huge losses.

words.meaning: When short-term rates are higher than long-term rates, often seen as a recession signal.
words.everyday: Like being paid more for a one-month savings account than a ten-year one.
words.work: An inverted yield curve has preceded most US recessions.
words.gap: Markets fretted over the ___.
words.plain: Short-term bonds pay more than long-term ones.

words.meaning: How sensitive a bond's price is to interest rate changes, roughly in years.
words.everyday: Like how far a seesaw tips: longer planks swing more.
words.work: Long-duration gilts fell 30% when rates rose.
words.gap: Bonds with high ___ fall more when rates rise.
words.plain: Long bonds lose much more value when rates go up.

words.meaning: Borrowing in a low-interest currency to invest in a higher-yielding one.
words.everyday: Like borrowing from a 0% card to put money in a 5% savings account.
words.work: The yen carry trade unwound violently.
words.gap: Investors borrowed yen to fund a ___.
words.plain: They borrowed cheaply in one currency to earn more in another.

words.meaning: The extra yield a corporate bond pays over a government bond, reflecting default risk.
words.everyday: Like the extra interest a friend with a patchy record must offer.
words.work: Credit spreads widened as recession fears grew.
words.gap: Wider ___s signal investors fear defaults.
words.plain: Investors want much more interest to lend to companies than to the government.

words.meaning: Valuing assets at current market prices rather than what was paid.
words.everyday: Like valuing your house at today's price, not what you paid in 2010.
words.work: Mark-to-market losses forced the bank to raise capital.
words.gap: ___ accounting showed the losses immediately.
words.plain: We value the bonds at today's prices, not the purchase price.

words.meaning: A private trading venue where large orders are hidden from the public market.
words.everyday: Like a private auction away from the main saleroom.
words.work: The pension fund sold the block in a dark pool.
words.gap: Big trades go through a ___ to avoid moving the price.
words.plain: They traded privately so the market wouldn't see the big order.
words.model: They traded in a dark pool.

words.meaning: The shares available for public trading, excluding those held by insiders.
words.everyday: Like the number of concert tickets actually on general sale.
words.work: A small free float makes the share volatile.
words.gap: Only 10% of the shares are in the ___.
words.plain: Only a small part of the shares can actually be traded.

words.meaning: A period after an IPO when insiders can't sell their shares.
words.everyday: Like a rule that new owners can't resell their tickets for six months.
words.work: Shares fell when the lock-up period expired.
words.gap: Employees can't sell during the ___.
words.plain: Insiders aren't allowed to sell for six months after listing.

words.meaning: Valuing an asset by estimating future cash and converting it to today's value.
words.everyday: Like valuing a buy-to-let flat by its future rents, worth less the further away they are.
words.work: Our discounted cash flow valuation is very sensitive to the growth rate.
words.gap: The analyst built a ___ model.
words.plain: We valued it by working out future cash and what it's worth today.
words.model: We used a discounted cash flow valuation.

words.meaning: The return investors expect for funding a company; the hurdle new projects must beat.
words.everyday: Like the interest you'd earn elsewhere, which a new venture must beat.
words.work: Higher rates raised our cost of capital.
words.gap: Projects must earn more than the ___.
words.plain: A project only makes sense if it returns more than our funding costs.
words.model: It must beat our cost of capital.

words.meaning: How much a share tends to move relative to the overall market.
words.everyday: Like how much a small boat rocks compared with the waves.
words.work: Tech stocks have a beta well above one.
words.gap: A share with a ___ of 2 moves twice as much as the market.
words.plain: This share swings twice as much as the market.
words.model: This share has a beta of two.

words.meaning: Return earned per unit of risk taken.
words.everyday: Like miles per gallon, but for investment risk.
words.work: The fund's Sharpe ratio is poor once you count its volatility.
words.gap: A higher ___ means better return for the risk.
words.plain: The fund's returns aren't great given how risky it is.
words.model: The fund has a low Sharpe ratio.

words.meaning: The tendency of prices or returns to drift back towards their long-run average.
words.everyday: Like an unusually hot week usually being followed by normal weather.
words.work: Value investors bet on mean reversion.
words.gap: Traders betting on ___ bought the fallen stock.
words.plain: Prices that move far from normal tend to come back.

words.meaning: The risk of rare, extreme losses.
words.everyday: Like the small chance of your house flooding badly.
words.work: Selling options earns steady income but carries tail risk.
words.gap: Hedge funds buy protection against ___.
words.plain: There's a small chance of a catastrophic loss.

words.meaning: The market's expectation of future price swings, read from option prices.
words.everyday: Like insurance prices rising before a storm.
words.work: Implied volatility spiked before the election.
words.gap: The VIX measures ___ on the S&P 500.
words.plain: Option prices show traders expect big swings.

words.meaning: A contract that pays out if a borrower defaults; insurance on debt.
words.everyday: Like insurance on a loan you made to a friend.
words.work: Credit default swaps on the bank's debt soared.
words.gap: Traders bought ___s to bet on a default.
words.plain: They bought insurance that pays out if the company can't repay.

words.meaning: Pooling loans, such as mortgages, and selling securities backed by them.
words.everyday: Like bundling hundreds of IOUs and selling shares in the bundle.
words.work: Securitisation spread subprime risk worldwide.
words.gap: Car loans are often sold through ___.
words.plain: The bank packaged lots of loans together and sold them to investors.

words.meaning: Periodic changes to an index's members or weights, forcing tracker funds to trade.
words.everyday: Like a league table update forcing fans to change their fantasy teams.
words.work: The share jumped ahead of index rebalancing.
words.gap: Tracker funds must buy on ___ day.
words.plain: Funds had to buy the share when it joined the index.
words.model: Index rebalancing forced funds to buy it.

words.meaning: Reducing debt, often by selling assets.
words.everyday: Like a household selling the second car to pay off loans.
words.work: Forced deleveraging drove prices down further.
words.gap: After the crash came years of ___.
words.plain: Everyone was selling assets to pay off what they owed.

words.meaning: A central bank signalling its likely future policy to steer expectations.
words.everyday: Like a teacher saying "no homework till Easter" so pupils plan ahead.
words.work: Forward guidance kept long-term rates low.
words.gap: The Bank used ___ to signal rates would stay low.
words.plain: The central bank said rates would stay low for a long time.
words.model: The central bank gave forward guidance.

words.meaning: Special purpose acquisition company: a listed shell that raises cash to buy a private firm.
words.everyday: Like an empty shop opened to buy a business it hasn't chosen yet.
words.work: The start-up went public by merging with a SPAC.
words.gap: The firm listed via a ___ rather than an IPO.
words.plain: They went public by merging with a listed shell company.
words.model: They went public via a SPAC.

words.meaning: How a bond's duration changes as rates change; more broadly, gaining more from good moves than you lose from bad.
words.everyday: Like a seesaw whose arm gets longer the further it tips your way.
words.work: Long bonds have high convexity.
words.gap: Options give a portfolio positive ___.
words.plain: The position gains more from good moves than it loses from bad ones.

words.meaning: When futures prices are higher than the current spot price.
words.everyday: Like paying more to book a holiday next year than to go now.
words.work: Oil was in steep contango as storage filled up.
words.gap: With the market in ___, rolling futures costs money.
words.plain: Oil for future delivery costs more than oil today.

words.meaning: When futures prices are lower than the current spot price, often due to shortages.
words.everyday: Like paying a premium for bread today in a shortage, with tomorrow's cheaper.
words.work: Gas went into backwardation during the shortage.
words.gap: Shortages pushed the market into ___.
words.plain: Gas today costs more than gas for future delivery.

words.meaning: Describing loans with few protective conditions for lenders.
words.everyday: Like lending to a friend without asking them to keep any savings or report their spending.
words.work: Covenant-lite loans left lenders exposed when profits fell.
words.gap: The boom saw a rise in ___ lending.
words.plain: The loan has hardly any conditions protecting the lender.

words.meaning: A reduction applied to the value of collateral or a debt.
words.everyday: Like a pawnshop lending only £80 against a £100 watch.
words.work: Bondholders took a 50% haircut in the restructuring.
words.gap: Lenders applied a 20% ___ to the bonds used as collateral.
words.plain: Creditors accepted getting back only half of what they lent.

words.meaning: Where firms borrow cash overnight by selling securities and agreeing to buy them back.
words.everyday: Like pawning your watch tonight and buying it back tomorrow.
words.work: The repo market froze in September 2019.
words.gap: Banks fund themselves daily in the ___.
words.plain: Banks borrow cash overnight by temporarily selling bonds.
words.model: Banks borrow in the repo market.

words.meaning: Collecting investor orders before an IPO to set the share price.
words.everyday: Like taking names and maximum bids before deciding a ticket price.
words.work: Strong book building let the bank raise the IPO price.
words.gap: The price range was raised during ___.
words.plain: The bank collected orders from investors to set the price.
words.model: The price was set through book building.

words.meaning: An option letting underwriters sell extra shares in an IPO to stabilise the price.
words.everyday: Like a venue keeping extra seats to release if demand is high.
words.work: The bank exercised the greenshoe option after strong demand.
words.gap: Underwriters used the ___ to sell 15% more shares.
words.plain: The bank was allowed to sell extra shares because demand was strong.
words.model: The bank exercised the greenshoe option.

words.meaning: The pattern where options far from the current price have higher implied volatility.
words.everyday: Like insurers charging extra for both very cheap and very expensive policies.
words.work: The volatility smile shows markets price in crashes.
words.gap: The ___ shows extreme moves are priced as more likely.
words.plain: Options for extreme price moves cost more than the models say they should.

words.meaning: Measures such as delta, gamma and vega that show how an option's price responds to changes.
words.everyday: Like a car's dashboard showing speed, acceleration and fuel use.
words.work: The desk hedges using the Greeks.
words.gap: Traders manage risk by watching ___.
words.plain: We measure how our options react to price, time and volatility.

words.meaning: A security backed by a pool of company loans, split into risk tranches.
words.everyday: Like a cake of loans cut into layers: the top layer is paid first.
words.work: Collateralised loan obligations buy most leveraged loans.
words.gap: Buyout loans are packaged into a ___.
words.plain: Company loans are pooled and sold in layers of risk.
words.model: They're packaged into a collateralised loan obligation.

words.meaning: The extra yield investors demand for holding long-term bonds instead of rolling short ones.
words.everyday: Like asking for more interest to lock savings away for ten years.
words.work: A rising term premium pushed up mortgage rates.
words.gap: Fiscal worries raised the ___ on long gilts.
words.plain: Investors want extra return for lending for longer.
